topics.title: Our Solar System's Family of Planets
passage: Our solar system consists of the sun and everything that orbits around it, including eight planets, dozens of moons, and countless smaller objects like asteroids and comets. The sun sits at the center, containing more than ninety-nine percent of all the mass in the entire solar system, with its powerful gravity holding every planet in a steady orbit around it.

The four planets closest to the sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are called terrestrial planets because they have solid, rocky surfaces similar in some ways to Earth's own ground. These planets are relatively small and dense compared to the planets farther out, and all four have gone through dramatic geological changes over billions of years, including volcanic activity and, in Earth's case, the movement of tectonic plates.

Beyond Mars lies a very different group of planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are called gas giants because they are made mostly of gas and lack a solid surface a person could stand on. Jupiter, the largest planet in the solar system, is so massive that more than one thousand Earths could fit inside it, while Saturn is famous for its spectacular rings made of countless chunks of ice and rock.

Between the rocky inner planets and the gas giants lies the asteroid belt, a region containing millions of rocky objects ranging in size from tiny pebbles to objects hundreds of miles wide. Scientists believe these asteroids are leftover material from the early formation of the solar system, material that never came together to form a full planet, giving researchers valuable clues about conditions billions of years ago.

Beyond Neptune lies an even more distant region called the Kuiper Belt, home to icy objects including the dwarf planet Pluto. Studying the solar system's most distant regions helps scientists understand how planets, moons, and smaller objects formed billions of years ago, and ongoing missions continue to send back new data that occasionally challenges what scientists thought they already knew.

topics.title: When Day Turns to Night: Solar and Lunar Eclipses
passage: An eclipse happens when one space object passes into the shadow of another, temporarily blocking light in a dramatic way visible from Earth. The two main types, solar eclipses and lunar eclipses, involve the same three objects, the sun, Earth, and the moon, but occur in different arrangements and produce very different sights in the sky.

A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes directly between the sun and Earth, blocking some or all of the sun's light from reaching a specific area on Earth's surface. During a total solar eclipse, the sky can darken dramatically in the middle of the day, and the sun's outer atmosphere, called the corona, becomes visible as a glowing ring around the darkened sun, a sight many describe as awe-inspiring.

A lunar eclipse happens the opposite way, when Earth passes directly between the sun and the moon, causing Earth's shadow to fall across the moon's surface. During a total lunar eclipse, the moon often takes on a reddish color rather than disappearing completely, because sunlight bending through Earth's atmosphere scatters most colors but lets red light pass through and reach the moon, an effect that has earned the nickname "blood moon."

Eclipses do not happen every month, even though the moon orbits Earth roughly every twenty-nine days, because the moon's orbit is slightly tilted compared to Earth's orbit around the sun. This means the sun, Earth, and moon only line up precisely enough for an eclipse a few times each year, making eclipses special events rather than a monthly occurrence.

Because a total solar eclipse is only visible from a narrow path on Earth's surface, while a lunar eclipse can be seen by anyone on the nighttime side of Earth at the same time, lunar eclipses are actually visible to far more people than solar eclipses. Scientists and eclipse enthusiasts often travel great distances to stand within the narrow path needed to witness a total solar eclipse in person.

options: Solar and lunar eclipses happen every single day.

topics.title: Stars and the Patterns We See
passage: On a clear night far from city lights, the sky can reveal thousands of stars, each one an enormous ball of burning gas producing its own light and heat, much like our sun. Stars appear as tiny points of light because they are almost unimaginably far away, with even the closest star beyond our sun located trillions of miles from Earth, a distance so large that scientists measure it using light-years instead of miles.

For thousands of years, people around the world have looked up at the night sky and noticed patterns formed by groups of stars, connecting them in their imaginations into shapes called constellations. Different cultures often saw different pictures in the same stars, creating their own stories and names, though today astronomers use an official, agreed-upon set of eighty-eight constellations to help organize and describe the sky.

Constellations served practical purposes long before modern navigation tools existed. Sailors used recognizable star patterns to figure out direction while at sea, and farmers used the appearance or disappearance of certain constellations throughout the year to know when to plant or harvest crops, since the visible stars change gradually as Earth orbits the sun.

Not all stars in the night sky are the same age, size, or color. Some stars burn hot and blue, living relatively short but intense lives, while others glow a cooler red and can burn steadily for tens of billions of years. Stars are born inside massive clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and depending on their size, they eventually die in very different ways, sometimes shrinking quietly and sometimes exploding in a dramatic burst called a supernova.

Today, scientists use powerful telescopes, some located on Earth and others orbiting in space, to study stars in far more detail than the naked eye ever could. Studying starlight helps scientists learn a star's temperature, composition, and distance from Earth, contributing to a broader understanding of how stars, and eventually entire galaxies, form and change over time.

options: Stars are all identical in size, color, and age.

topics.title: Comets and Meteor Showers
passage: Comets are chunks of ice, dust, and rock that travel through the solar system on long, looping orbits around the sun, often taking many years or even centuries to complete a single trip. As a comet gets closer to the sun, heat causes some of its icy surface to turn directly into gas, releasing dust and gas that form a glowing cloud around the comet's core and often a long, bright tail that can stretch for millions of miles.

A comet's tail always points away from the sun, no matter which direction the comet is traveling, because it is pushed by solar wind and light pressure from the sun rather than trailing behind the comet like smoke behind a car. This means that when a comet is moving away from the sun, its tail actually leads in front of it rather than following behind, which often surprises people learning about comets for the first time.

Meteor showers are closely connected to comets, since they often happen when Earth passes through a trail of dust and debris left behind by a comet's previous visits to the inner solar system. When these tiny particles, most no larger than a grain of sand, enter Earth's atmosphere at high speed, friction causes them to burn up, creating the streaks of light commonly called shooting stars.

Because Earth passes through the same debris trails at roughly the same time every year, meteor showers are predictable annual events that skywatchers can plan for in advance. During a strong meteor shower, observers in a dark location with a clear sky might see dozens of meteors per hour, though light pollution from cities can make even a strong shower difficult to see clearly.

Occasionally, a piece of debris large enough to survive the trip through Earth's atmosphere reaches the ground, and scientists call the remaining object a meteorite. Studying meteorites gives scientists valuable information about the materials that existed when the solar system first formed billions of years ago, since some meteorites are older than any rock found naturally on Earth's surface.

questions.question: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Comets and meteor showers are unrelated phenomena with no connection to each other.
Comets leave behind debris trails that create predictable meteor showers, and studying related meteorites reveals clues about the early solar system.
Meteor showers happen randomly with no yearly pattern at all.
Comets only appear once and are never seen again.
